<reason>Both sides were disciplined (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure, no fake sourcing, real clash), but PRO built the more durable route to victory. CON's best move was the category-vs-risk dilemma (the motion empowers islands by geography but is defended by risk logic) plus the "moral theater" enforcement objection. PRO's Rebuttal 2 dissolved the dilemma by anchoring the metric in the motion's own word "existential" — annihilation of statehood (Tuvalu) versus catastrophic but partial loss (Bangladesh) — making the swamping/arbitrariness fork collapse. On enforcement, PRO showed CON's demand ("name one provision emitters would implement against their will") proves too much since it applies to every treaty rule including the consensus CON defends (and the US quit Paris under consensus), then offered a positive mechanism: outvoted text becomes the baseline that litigation, border adjustments, and finance conditions bite on. CON's counters — "rigging by definition" and "those levers exist today" — were sharp but only half-answered baseline authorship, and CON never resolved the asymmetry PRO pressed: demanding guarantees of the reform that the failed status quo cannot meet either. PRO made the debate easier to decide; CON's excellent rhetoric outran its answered objections.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2: A1's "annihilation versus injury" reading of existential risk directly neutralized CON's Q1 and opening dilemma, while A2 converted CON's enforcement challenge into a proves-too-much plus the "price of defiance" baseline mechanism; runner-up is B2.7's "they won a sentence" flip of CON's AOSIS/Paris point.</best_rebuttal>
